stories.headline: What does Murasu mean? The story behind the cyclone heading towards Andhra
stories.title: What does Murasu mean? The story behind the cyclone heading towards Andhra
stories.summary: What does Murasu mean? The story behind the cyclone heading towards Andhra
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: The IMD named the Andhra-bound cyclonic storm Murasu after Cyclone Arnab.
The sequence reflects a regional system rather than the storm's destination or intensity.
A cyclone heading towards Andhra Pradesh has a name that sounds more like a call to battle than a weather warning.
Called Murasu, the storm has drawn its name from Tamil, where the word refers to a large drum traditionally used during war, celebrations and to alert people to impending danger.
The name has also followed a specific sequence.
Days after Cyclone Arnab, which was named by Bangladesh, made landfall in Andhra Pradesh on October 28, the India Meteorological Department (IMD) named the next cyclonic storm Murasu.
India had contributed the name to the regional list.
So, how did an Andhra-bound cyclone get a Tamil name, and who decides what a storm should be called?
WHY IS THE CYCLONE CALLED MURASU?
Murasu is a Tamil word referring to a musical instrument, specifically a large drum.
Traditionally, the instrument has been associated with different public and social occasions, including warfare, celebrations and alerting people to imminent danger.
The drum was used to communicate important messages, summon people and signal events.

stories.title: Cyclone Murasu nears Andhra coast, heavy rain floods Chennai; flights cancelled
stories.summary: Cyclone Murasu nears Andhra coast, heavy rain floods Chennai; flights cancelled
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: Severe cyclone Murasu brought heavy rain to Chennai while approaching the south Andhra Pradesh coast.
The downpour disrupted flights and schools, prompting civic teams to tackle waterlogging.
Heavy rain lashed northern Tamil Nadu and flooded several parts of Chennai as severe Cyclone Murasu moved towards the south Andhra Pradesh coast, news agency Press Trust of India reported.
Some flights at Chennai airport were cancelled on Monday because of adverse weather.
Passengers were advised to contact their airlines for further information and assistance.
The India Meteorological Department issued an orange alert for Chennai, while schools in the city were closed for the day.
Several parts of Chennai, Chengalpattu and Tiruvallur districts have received torrential rain since Sunday night.
In the past 24 hours, Madhavaram recorded 11 cm of rain, while Ennore Port and Nungambakkam recorded 10 cm each, an official told PTI.
An orange alert indicates very heavy rainfall of between 11 cm and 20 cm.
Greater Chennai Corporation Commissioner GS Sameeran said there was no major flooding, though some areas had reported minor water stagnation.
He oversaw the civic body's operation to pump out water from inundated areas.
"Out of 22 subways in the city, two faced a minor waterlogging issue, and the water was soon cleared for traffic," Sameeran told reporters on Monday, according to PTI.

stories.headline: Odisha CM announces special package for families affected by Cyclone Arnab
stories.title: Odisha CM announces special package for families affected by Cyclone Arnab
stories.summary: After reviewing the prevailing flood situation in the State in the evening, CM Majhi said people in several districts, especially Ganjam, Gajapati and Kandhamal, were affected by cyclone Arnab and its aftermath of heavy rainfall
reasons: source: event has 2 copies, primary source counted once
corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: Odisha Chief Minister Mohan Charan Majhi on Sunday (October 2, 2026) announced a special package of 50kg of rice and ₹2,500 for every family affected by the recent rain and flood in the southern districts, besides damages for losses to crops and property due to Cyclone Arnab.
With another cyclonic storm expected to hit the coasts of Andhra Pradesh, the Chief Minister said the relief package will be reviewed again upon assessing damage after the weather system passes.

After reviewing the prevailing flood situation in the State in the evening, CM Majhi said people in several districts, especially Ganjam, Gajapati and Kandhamal, were affected by cyclone Arnab and its aftermath of heavy rainfall.

“Thousands of acres of crops and several houses have been damaged,” he told reporters and pointed out that assessment of damage was underway while the primary task was relief distribution and restoration.
"I am hopeful that normalcy will return in affected areas in the next one or two days as the administration is taking all necessary measures," he said.
The Chief Minister announced that all affected families will get 50kg of rice and ₹2,500 in cash.

Small and marginal farmers, who sustained crop loss of 33% and above, will receive an agricultural input subsidy of ₹8,500 per hectare of land in rain-fed and non-irrigated areas, while ₹17,000 per hectare of land will be provided for areas under assured irrigation, he said.

Similarly, assistance for perennial crops like mango and cashew will be ₹22,500 per hectare, the Chief Minister said, adding that a minimum agricultural input subsidy of ₹2500 will be given to any affected farmer for perennial crops and ₹1000 for non-irrigated areas.
"The government will provide ₹18,000 to each affected farmer to remove sand and silt from the fields.
The State will also provide 1.75 lakh mini kits to farmers for free," he added.

Under the housing sector, he said assistance of ₹1.20 lakh will be given for fully damaged houses in the plains, ₹1.30 lakh in hilly areas, while ₹6,500 and ₹4,000 will be given for partially damaged pucca and kutcha houses, respectively.
CM Majhi said his government has decided to provide compensation of ₹10,000 for affected small shops, street vendors and kiosks and ₹25,000 for affected big shops and commercial establishments.

article_sentences: The northeast monsoon has finally arrived in Tamil Nadu.
Chennai experienced an average rainfall of 76.07 mm in the 24 hours until 6 a.m. on November 2, according to the Chennai Corporation’s Integrated Command and Control Centre (ICCC).
Of the monitoring stations, 28 of them recorded heavy rainfall, and five recorded very heavy rainfall, with no location reporting extremely heavy rainfall.
In Chennai, Parrys in Royapuram Zone recorded highest rainfall of 149.2 mm, followed by New Manali Town 141.6 mm, Manali (Ward 18) 136.2 mm, New Manali Town (Ward 15) 131.2 mm and Manali 129.9 mm.
Chennai city recorded an average rainfall of 76.07 mm in the 24 hours ending at 6 a.m. on November 2, according to Chennai Corporation"s Integrated Command and Control Centre (ICCC).
Of the monitoring stations, 28 recorded heavy rainfall and five recorded very heavy rainfall.
No location reported extremely heavy rainfall.

Parrys in Royapuram Zone (5) recorded the highest rainfall at 149.2 mm, followed by New Manali Town (141.6 mm), Manali (Ward 18) (136.2 mm), New Manali Town (Ward 15) (131.2 mm) and Manali (129.9 mm).
Northern areas, including Manali, Ennore, Kathivakkam, Tiruvottiyur, Madhavaram and Puzhal, received over 100 mm of rainfall at several locations.

article_sentences: Kerala issues yellow weather alerts across multiple districts as Cyclone Murasu heads towards Andhra Pradesh, bringing heavy rainfall to the state until Wednesday.
Thiruvananthapuram: Following Arnab, another cyclone is heading towards Andhra Pradesh.
Although it will not directly hit Kerala, heavy rainfall is likely across the state until Wednesday.
The storm has been named 'Murasu', a title submitted by India.
The cyclone formed over the Bay of Bengal, 630 km east-southeast of Chennai.
It is expected to intensify into a severe cyclonic storm on Monday and make landfall between Nellore and Narsapur in Andhra Pradesh early on Tuesday, with wind speeds reaching up to 120 km/h.
On Monday (November 2), a yellow warning for heavy rain was issued for six districts in Kerala: Palakkad, Malappuram, Kozhikode, Wayanad, Kannur and Kasaragod.
On Tuesday (November 3), the yellow warning applies to Kozhikode, Wayanad, Kannur and Kasaragod districts.
And on Wednesday (November 4), it covers Pathanamthitta, Idukki, Palakkad and Malappuram districts.

stories.headline: Cyclone Murasu | Paddy farmers in Telangana fear crop damage amid high market prices
stories.title: Cyclone Murasu | Paddy farmers in Telangana fear crop damage amid high market prices
stories.summary: With soaked panicles delaying harvest, higher machine costs, and the need for extra drying and labor, growers warn that pre-flowering crops could suffer more, even as authorities issue alerts and supply protective tarpaulins to cushion the impact
reasons: source: event has 2 copies, primary source counted once
corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: The rain forecast under the impact of cyclonic storm Murasu (war drum) in various districts of Telangana from Monday to Wednesday (November 2 to 4) is giving jitters to farmers whose paddy and cotton crops are in various stages of cultivation.
According to farmers, when rice panicles get soaked in rain and droops, machines used for harvesting paddy have to be hired for some more time, which results in spending more money.
The soaked produce has to be dried, which may result in loss of some weight.
Labour also need to be hired to channel water away from damaged paddy crops.
And those in the pre-flowering stage might suffer greater damage.
Currently, paddy crops are in various stages — depending on the time of sowing — ranging from harvest, nearing harvest and pre-flowering stage.

The cyclonic storm is posing a threat to farmers at a time when they are getting relatively more prices for harvest — ranging from ₹3,500 to ₹4,500 per quintal of fresh produce, against around ₹2,900 (MSP and ₹500 bonus for fine rice) of dried crop earlier.
Cotton crops, which are nearing harvest, may suffer similar damage.

Sankranthi Narasiah, a paddy farmer from Lalapuram village, Konijerla mandal, Khammam, said that his and other crops around him are in various stages — ranging from pre-flowering to panicle formation.
“Wind and rain in this stage will cause us great loss,” said Mr. Narsaiah.
Khammam is one of the six districts forecast to receive heavy to very heavy rainfall on Monday (November 2, 2026).
Mahabubnagar, Nalgonda, Suryapet, Nagarkurnool and Wanaparthy are the remaining five.

stories.headline: Kulgam quake puts Kashmir’s seismic risk in focus
stories.title: Kulgam quake puts Kashmir’s seismic risk in focus
stories.summary: Srinagar, Nov 1: A 3.6-magnitude earthquake in south Kashmir’s Kulgam district has brought renewed attention to the seismic risks facing the valley, where active faults and complex geological structures make large areas vulnerable to earthquakes. Earth scientists say detailed mapping of local hazards, safer construction and preparedness are essential to limit the damage from future earthquakes. The earthquake struck DamhalHanjipora at 1:00:46 am on Friday at a depth of 10 km, according to the National Centre for Seismology (NCS). Its epicentre was recorded at latitude 33.628° N and longitude 74.922° E. Prof Shakil Ahmad Romshoo, eminent earth scientist and Vice Chancellor of the Islamic University of Science and Technology (IUST), said the tremor was a reminder of Kashmir’s active tectonic setting. “Although an earthquake of this magnitude is minor, its shallow depth made the tremors perceptible in nearby areas,” Romshoo said. “Such earthquakes are not unusual in the seismically active Kashmir Himalaya and should be interpreted as part of the region’s larger seismicity.” He said earthquakes could not be predicted in terms of their timing, location or magnitude. “Preparedness, establishing a culture of disaster preparedness and risk-reduction measures are our most effective safeguards against future earthquake disasters,” Prof Ramshoo said. Riyaz Ahmad Mir, a scientist at the National Institute of Hydrology’s Western Himalayan Regional Centre (WHRC), Jammu, said several regional and local faults, thrusts and other active tectonic structures traverse Kashmir. “DH Pora, Kulgam, is no exception. The area is influenced by tectonic structures such as the Balapur Fault and Jhelum Fault. Furthermore, the southwestern PirPanjal is considered tectonically active, adding to the regional seismic hazard,” Mir said. The Balapur Fault is a reverse or thrust fault, where pressure pushes one block of the Earth’s crust over another. The Jhelum Fault is a strike-slip fault, along which blocks of the crust move horizontally past each other. Mir said the risk at a particular location depends on its proximity to faults, geological conditions, site characteristics and the vulnerability of buildings and infrastructure. Much of Kashmir falls in Seismic Zone V, the highest earthquake hazard category under India’s current classification. Parts of the Chenab Valley - Doda, Ramban and Kishtwar districts in the Jammu region— also fall in Zone V, while areas including the PirPanjal region - Rajouri and Poonch -are classified under Zone IV. The Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS) ’IS 1893:2016 divides the country into four seismic zones; II, III, IV, and V. Zone IV denotes high seismic hazard, while Zone V denotes very high hazard. Zone VI was proposed in the revised seismic zonation in 2025 to represent the exceptionally high earthquake hazard of the Himalayan region but was subsequently withdrawn. Mir said the Himalaya was a continuous, tectonically active mountain belt largely governed by the Main Himalayan Thrust (MHT), but earthquake hazard varied across the range. “Seismic zoning divides the region based on differences in expected ground shaking, earthquake potential, tectonic segmentation, local fault systems, geological conditions and historical seismicity,” he said. Mir said broad regional classifications could overlook local differences in risk, even within the same seismic zone. “The presence of a common active tectonic system does not imply identical seismic hazard everywhere. However, broad regional zoning may oversimplify local variations,” he said. He called for detailed seismic microzonation and active fault mapping to assess earthquake risk across the Himalaya. The experts also called for strict enforcement of earthquake-resistant building codes, assessment of vulnerable structures and regular safety drills in schools and public institutions.

“Such earthquakes are not unusual in the seismically active Kashmir Himalaya and should be interpreted as part of the region’s larger seismicity.” He said earthquakes could not be predicted in terms of their timing, location or magnitude.
“Preparedness, establishing a culture of disaster preparedness and risk-reduction measures are our most effective safeguards against future earthquake disasters,” Prof Ramshoo said.

Riyaz Ahmad Mir, a scientist at the National Institute of Hydrology’s Western Himalayan Regional Centre (WHRC), Jammu, said several regional and local faults, thrusts and other active tectonic structures traverse Kashmir.
“DH Pora, Kulgam, is no exception.
The area is influenced by tectonic structures such as the Balapur Fault and Jhelum Fault.
Furthermore, the southwestern PirPanjal is considered tectonically active, adding to the regional seismic hazard,” Mir said.
The Balapur Fault is a reverse or thrust fault, where pressure pushes one block of the Earth’s crust over another.
The Jhelum Fault is a strike-slip fault, along which blocks of the crust move horizontally past each other.
Mir said the risk at a particular location depends on its proximity to faults, geological conditions, site characteristics and the vulnerability of buildings and infrastructure.
Much of Kashmir falls in Seismic Zone V, the highest earthquake hazard category under India’s current classification.

Parts of the Chenab Valley - Doda, Ramban and Kishtwar districts in the Jammu region— also fall in Zone V, while areas including the PirPanjal region - Rajouri and Poonch -are classified under Zone IV.
The Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS) ’IS 1893:2016 divides the country into four seismic zones; II, III, IV, and V. Zone IV denotes high seismic hazard, while Zone V denotes very high hazard.
Zone VI was proposed in the revised seismic zonation in 2025 to represent the exceptionally high earthquake hazard of the Himalayan region but was subsequently withdrawn.
Mir said the Himalaya was a continuous, tectonically active mountain belt largely governed by the Main Himalayan Thrust (MHT), but earthquake hazard varied across the range.

“Seismic zoning divides the region based on differences in expected ground shaking, earthquake potential, tectonic segmentation, local fault systems, geological conditions and historical seismicity,” he said.
Mir said broad regional classifications could overlook local differences in risk, even within the same seismic zone.
“The presence of a common active tectonic system does not imply identical seismic hazard everywhere.
However, broad regional zoning may oversimplify local variations,” he said.
He called for detailed seismic microzonation and active fault mapping to assess earthquake risk across the Himalaya.
The experts also called for strict enforcement of earthquake-resistant building codes, assessment of vulnerable structures and regular safety drills in schools and public institutions.

stories.headline: Supreme Court Dismisses Ex-TN Minister KN Nehru's Plea Against HC Direction For FIR Registration On ED Materials
stories.title: Supreme Court Dismisses Ex-TN Minister KN Nehru's Plea Against HC Direction For FIR Registration On ED Materials
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'supreme court' in title weight 44
article_sentences: The Supreme Court on Monday dismissed a plea filed by former Tamil Nadu Minister KN Nehru challenging a Madras High Court direction to register an FIR against him on corruption allegations based on materials shared by the Enforcement Directorate (ED).

A bench comprising Justice Dipankar Datta and Justice Sheel Nagu observed that there was no ground made out to interfere with the High Court's February 20 judgment and its October 26 order dismissing Nehru's review petition.

The bench clarified that the High Court's observations will be considered as necessary only for the purpose of the disposal of the matters, and will not preclude the petitioner from raising his defence at the appropriate stage.

The matter pertains to alleged irregularities in recruitment to 2,538 posts in the Tamil Nadu Municipal Administration and Water Supply Department, involving alleged illegal gratification of approximately ₹634 crore.
The ED had forwarded materials to the Tamil Nadu Director General of Police in October 2025, alleging corruption in the recruitment process.
Senior Advocate Shyam Divan, for Nehru, submitted that the High Court's order was fundamentally erroneous as it was passed without giving him an opportunity of hearing.
Divan said that had the High Court merely ordered an investigation, it would still have been acceptable; however, the High Court passed adverse findings against him without hearing him.
The bench however pointed out that he was served notice but did not join the proceedings.
Divan said that notice was received on the day when the matter was reserved for hearing, and there was no effective opportunity to file a response.
Justice Datta also disagreed that there was any finding by the High Court, and that they were merely recording the observations in the record.

On merits, Divan argued that the ECIR was quashed by the Madras High Court in July 2025 as the predicate offence was earlier quashed, and once the ECIR has gone, the ED cannot invoke Section 66(2) of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act to share the information with the State police.
"The moment the predicate offence is quashed, and ECIR is set aside, this expression 'material in his possession' doesn't apply because they don't have anything in their possession.

stories.headline: Kerala High Court's Example Prompted Supreme Court To Strive For More Women Representation : CJI Surya Kant
stories.title: Kerala High Court's Example Prompted Supreme Court To Strive For More Women Representation : CJI Surya Kant
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'supreme court' in title weight 44
article_sentences: Chief Justice of India Surya Kant on Sunday (November 1) inaugurated the Platinum Jubilee Celebration of the Kerala High Court, marking 70 years since its inception on November 1, 1956.

"This High Court has been a place where constitutional promises have found practical meaning, where difficult questions of law have received thoughtful answers, and where successive generations have reposed their faith in the ideals of justice, fairness and dignity.
It is this legacy of public trust and constitutional commitment that makes today's occasion truly worthy of celebration..
I am, therefore, specially pleased that this historic occasion has finally brought me to this beautiful State," Justice Kant began his inaugural address.

"It seems to me that after I took over as Chief Justice of India, the collegium must have been influenced by this pragmatic and progressive approach of the Kerala High Court as we have been able to bring two distinguished women judges to Supreme Court in the recent time.

May be, somewhere behind the back of my mind, I must have been influenced with the visionary approach of this High Court where on judicial side, I was able to, not only pass an order, but persuade the majority of the State Bar Councils, the Bar Council of India and the District and High Court Bar Associations to ensure 30% representation for the women members of the bar.

All these historical steps find their strength and legacy somewhere and for that I will give full credit to the Kerala High Court because it was this High Court that at a time when the higher judiciary remained largely dominated by men or when the Bar Associations or the Bar Council were on the lighter side named as 'Men Club', I think the example set by this High Court has prompted and persuaded the Apex institution of this country to provide a formidable, fair and effective representation to the women members of the bar, whether it was a question of bench or the question of effective representation in Bar Council and Bar Associations."
Justice Kant also emphasised upon the High Courts' power to uphold constitutional and legal rights of the people, with a touch that can only provided by institutions closer to them.
He pointed to a 'new dimension of litigation' where litigants approach the Supreme Court for urgent listings before the High Courts.
He added that timely intervention and interim orders are often more important than final verdicts, and High Courts must strive to recognise the same.
"The Supreme Court, on its side, has consistently respected the institutional autonomy of the High Courts, including their authority to regulate their own rosters.
That position is rooted in respect for the constitutional status of the High Courts.

stories.headline: Karnataka issues final land acquisition notification for Greater Bengaluru township
stories.title: Karnataka issues final land acquisition notification for Greater Bengaluru township
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: The Karnataka government has issued the final land acquisition notification for 1,895 acres in Kanchugaranahalli and Byramangala villages of Bidadi Hobli in Ramanagara taluk for the proposed Greater Bengaluru Integrated Township (GBIT).

The October 30 notification identifies 3,271 landowners whose compensation will be determined under the Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation, and Resettlement Act, 2013.
Landowners can also opt for developed sites in lieu of monetary compensation.
The Greater Bengaluru Development Authority (GBDA), which is implementing the project, plans to develop the township under a ‘work-live-play’ model.
The proposed township is planned across villages between Bidadi and Harohalli in Bengaluru South district.
It has faced sustained opposition from farmers and local residents for over a year, who fear losing agricultural land and their livelihoods.
Earlier in August, the state government constituted a four-member committee headed by Justice Guhanathan Narendar to examine the differing views on the Bidadi Township project.
The committee was tasked with examining the project’s legal, humanitarian, and developmental aspects and submitting its recommendations to the government.
Farmers in the affected villages said they would continue opposing the acquisition.

Nagaraj MR of the Byramangala and Kanchugaranahalli Farmers’ Land Rights Protection Association said the final notification was issued even before a government-appointed review committee submitted its report.
Nagaraj also alleged that farmers were threatened with litigation and pressured to accept compensation and give up their land.

The township proposal received Cabinet approval in January 2025, following which the GBDA issued a preliminary land acquisition notification in March 2025, proposing to acquire 7,481 acres across nine villages.
